stichs.en: Make my steps firm by Your word,
and let no iniquity rule over me.

verses.summary: Two requests in one breath, and they pull in opposite directions: hold the feet steady, and hold something else back. The Torah word is imrah, the spoken promise, used here as the ground underfoot rather than as something studied.

stichs.en: Redeem me from the oppression of man,
and I will keep Your precepts.

verses.summary: The pressure named in the previous verse was iniquity from within; here it is a human hand from outside. The consequence clause is the same shape both times: rescue first, then keeping. This one uses piqqudim.

stichs.en: Make Your face shine upon Your servant,
and teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: Light and instruction asked for as one thing. The vocabulary of the first half is the vocabulary of the priestly blessing; the second half turns that light into a lesson, and the word is chuqqim.

stichs.en: Streams of water run down from my eyes,
because they have not kept Your teaching.

verses.summary: The subject of the failing verb is an unnamed they, never identified. The weeping is not over the speaker's own trouble, which is what makes this verse unusual in a psalm otherwise spoken in the first person. Torah.

stichs.en: You are righteous, O LORD,
and Your judgments are upright.

verses.summary: The tzade stanza opens by conceding the verdict before any request is made. Both halves are verbless clauses, an adjective set beside a noun, which is how Hebrew states what simply is the case. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: You have commanded Your testimonies in righteousness,
and in great faithfulness.

verses.summary: The testimonies are not described here, they are commanded: the verb makes them an act performed rather than a document held. Righteousness and faithfulness are the manner of the commanding, not properties of the text. Edot.

stichs.en: My zeal has consumed me,
because my foes have forgotten Your words.

verses.summary: The damage is self-inflicted and the cause is other people. Zeal is the subject of the verb and the speaker is its object, which is a precise way of saying that caring about this is costing him. Devarim.

stichs.en: Your word is refined through and through,
and Your servant loves it.

verses.summary: The image is metallurgical: the participle is what is done to silver in a crucible. The love in the second half follows from the testing, not from sentiment. The suffix on the last verb is feminine, agreeing with imrah.

stichs.en: I am small and despised,
yet I have not forgotten Your precepts.

verses.summary: Social standing on one side, memory on the other, joined without any word for yet: the contrast is carried by juxtaposition alone. The same denial of forgetting will close the whole psalm. Piqqudim.

stichs.en: Your righteousness is righteousness forever,
and Your teaching is truth.

verses.summary: Four nouns and no verb in the entire verse. Nothing is claimed about what Torah does; two identities are asserted and left standing. Torah, paired with the abstract noun for truth.

stichs.en: Distress and anguish have found me,
yet Your commandments are my delight.

verses.summary: The tzade sounds crowd together in the first half, three words in a row built on the same consonant, so the line sounds pinched before it says it is. The word for delight returns at verse 174. Mitzvot.

stichs.en: Your testimonies are righteous forever;
give me understanding, that I may live.

verses.summary: The stanza ends by turning its own statement into a demand. What is true forever is no use until it is understood, and understanding is set as the condition of living, not its reward. Edot.

stichs.en: I have called with my whole heart;
answer me, O LORD;
I will keep Your statutes.

verses.summary: The qof stanza is built on the root for calling and the root for drawing near, and this is the first of two consecutive verses whose opening verb is a call. Note that the object comes before its verb in the last two words. Chuqqim.

stichs.en: I have called You: save me,
and I will keep Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Four words, one of the four shortest verses in the psalm. The object suffix on the first verb means the call is already addressed before anything is asked for. Edot, and the same promise clause as verse 134.

stichs.en: I was up before dawn and cried out;
I have hoped in Your word.

verses.summary: The verb does not mean to rise early, it means to get ahead of something, and what is outrun here is the daybreak. This is the only time stamp in the stanza. Davar.

stichs.en: My eyes got ahead of the night watches,
to meditate on Your word.

verses.summary: The same verb as the previous verse, now with the eyes as its subject rather than the whole person. The purpose is given by an infinitive, which is rare here: most verses state a promise instead. Imrah.

stichs.en: Hear my voice according to Your kindness, O LORD;
according to Your justice, revive me.

verses.summary: Two matched ke- prefixes set the measure of the request, first covenant kindness and then legal judgment, as if either standard would do. Revive me runs four times through this last quarter of the psalm. Mishpat.

stichs.en: Those who chase after scheming have drawn near;
they are far from Your teaching.

verses.summary: Near and far in one line, and the two verbs sit at opposite ends of the verse so the distance is visible on the page. This sets the trap the next verse springs. Torah.

stichs.en: You are near, O LORD,
and all Your commandments are truth.

verses.summary: The answer to the previous verse reuses its adjective: the pursuers are near, and so is God, and the psalm lets the two nearnesses stand side by side without ranking them. Mitzvot.

stichs.en: Long ago I learned from Your testimonies
that You founded them forever.

verses.summary: The testimonies are the source of the knowledge and also its object, so the claim is self-supporting by design. The closing verb is the one used for laying a foundation. Edot.

stichs.en: See my affliction and rescue me,
for I have not forgotten Your teaching.

verses.summary: The resh stanza opens with an imperative of looking, and the same imperative opens verse 159, bracketing the stanza. The ground offered is memory rather than merit. Torah.

stichs.en: Argue my case and redeem me;
revive me according to Your word.

verses.summary: A verb and its own noun stacked together, the construction Hebrew uses to say plead the plea. The vocabulary is a lawsuit in the first half and a family redeemer in the second. Imrah, first of three groundings for revive me in this stanza.

stichs.en: Salvation is far from the wicked,
for they have not sought Your statutes.

verses.summary: The far and near pairing from verse 150 returns, now applied to rescue rather than to people. The distance is presented as a consequence of not seeking, not as a punishment imposed. Chuqqim.

stichs.en: Your compassions are many, O LORD;
revive me according to Your judgments.

verses.summary: Second of the three revive me requests in this stanza, and each one names a different measure: word here becomes judgments, and will become kindness at verse 159. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: My pursuers and my foes are many,
yet I have not turned aside from Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Many is the first word of this verse and the second word of the last one, so mercies and persecutors are counted with the same adjective. The verb is spatial: not turning off a road. Edot.

stichs.en: I saw traitors and I contended with them,
because they did not keep Your word.

verses.summary: The middle verb is rare and its force is disputed: translations divide between quarrelling with them and being sickened by them. Either way the reaction is provoked by watching, not by being harmed. Imrah.

stichs.en: See how I love Your precepts;
O LORD, revive me according to Your kindness.

verses.summary: The look demanded at verse 153 is demanded again, closing the stanza, but now what is to be looked at is affection rather than affliction. Third revive me, this one measured by chesed. Piqqudim.

stichs.en: The sum of Your word is truth,
and every judgment of Your righteousness stands forever.

verses.summary: The first noun means head, and readers split over whether it points to the beginning of the word or to its total. Both readings are defended; the psalm does not settle it. Davar closing a stanza that began with Torah.

stichs.en: Princes have hunted me without cause,
but my heart dreads Your word.

verses.summary: The stanza opens by moving fear off its obvious target. Powerful men are chasing him and the thing his heart shakes at is a word. Davar, with the prefix meaning at or because of.

stichs.en: I rejoice over Your word
like one who finds great spoil.

verses.summary: The only simile in this stretch of the psalm, and it is taken from the battlefield: plunder found after the fighting, not wages earned. Great returns as the first adjective of verse 165. Imrah.

stichs.en: Falsehood I hate and abhor;
Your teaching I love.

verses.summary: Both halves put the object first and the verb second, so the sentence turns on the pivot between two hate verbs and one love verb. Nothing is asked for in this verse. Torah.

stichs.en: Seven times a day I have praised You,
for the judgments of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: The only counted quantity in the stanza, and the number has been read both as a literal tally and as a round figure for completeness. The last two words are a chain of two nouns, judgments belonging to righteousness. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: Great peace belongs to those who love Your teaching,
and nothing makes them stumble.

verses.summary: The word for them here is an archaic poetic form, not the ordinary one, which is part of why this line reads as a formula rather than a report. The noun for stumbling block occurs only here in the psalm. Torah.

stichs.en: I have waited for Your salvation, O LORD,
and I have done Your commandments.

verses.summary: Waiting and acting reported in the same tense, side by side, with no suggestion that one is preparation for the other. The verb for hoping is uncommon. Mitzvot.

stichs.en: My soul has kept Your testimonies,
and I love them very much.

verses.summary: The keeping is credited to the nefesh rather than to the speaker, which puts the obedience below the level of decision. The plural object suffix on the love verb points back to the testimonies. Edot.

stichs.en: I have kept Your precepts and Your testimonies,
for all my ways are in front of You.

verses.summary: Two of the eight Torah words share one clause here, piqqudim and edot joined by a conjunction rather than split across the two halves. The reason given for obeying is being watched, not being rewarded.

stichs.en: Let my cry come near before You, O LORD;
give me understanding according to Your word.

verses.summary: The tav stanza is almost entirely jussive: let this happen, let that happen. The verb for drawing near is the one from the qof stanza, now applied to the speaker's own shout. Davar.

stichs.en: Let my plea come before You;
deliver me according to Your word.

verses.summary: Built on the same frame as the verse before it, with imrah swapped in for davar and rescue asked for instead of understanding. The pairing of the two synonyms across adjacent verses is deliberate.

stichs.en: Let my lips pour out praise,
for You teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: The opening verb is used of a spring bubbling up, so the praise is asked for as something involuntary. Teaching is stated as ongoing rather than requested. Chuqqim.

stichs.en: Let my tongue answer with Your word,
for all Your commandments are righteousness.

verses.summary: The verb can mean answer or sing out, and both senses are in play here. Lips in the previous verse, tongue in this one: the organs of speech are asked for one at a time. Imrah and mitzvot in the same verse.

stichs.en: Let Your hand be there to help me,
for I have chosen Your precepts.

verses.summary: The ground offered is an act of will, and the verb for choosing appears only twice in the whole psalm, here and at verse 30. Everywhere else the speaker pleads memory or love instead. Piqqudim.

stichs.en: I have longed for Your salvation, O LORD,
and Your teaching is my delight.

verses.summary: Salvation echoes verse 166 and delight echoes verse 143, so the last stanza is gathering its own earlier vocabulary. Longing is stated as a completed act. Torah.

stichs.en: Let my soul live, and let it praise You,
and let Your judgments help me.

verses.summary: Living is asked for with a purpose attached, which is unusual: the request is not to survive but to be able to say something. In the second half the judgments become the agents of the help. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: I have strayed like a lost sheep;
seek out Your servant,
for I have not forgotten Your commandments.

verses.summary: One hundred and seventy five verses of keeping, and the last one admits to being lost. The imperative asks God to do the searching, and the final clause is the same denial of forgetting used at verses 141 and 153. Mitzvot.
